about: Next-occurrence computation. Every case gives a rule, a completion event, and the expected next instance. These are the cases where real implementations disagree today.

cases.why: February is skipped, not absorbed. This is what RRULE with BYMONTHDAY=31 does, and what EventKit does. A tool that returns 2026-02-28 here has silently changed the user's rule.

Clamping is a legitimate behavior and many tools do it. It is only a bug when undeclared. Both this case and the one above must pass — the format does not pick a winner, it requires producers to say which they do.

The most common clamping bug. Clamping to Feb 28 must not move the series to the 28th permanently — the rule is still 'the 31st', and March has one. Implementations that advance from the clamped date rather than from the rule degrade a month-end task to the 28th forever after one February, and the user is never told.

Completion-anchored recurrence is a function of history, not of time. The date of occurrence N+2 depends on when the user completes N+1, which has not happened. A producer claiming to have materialized three instances ahead is claiming to know something unknowable.
Four weeks after the haircut you actually got, not four weeks after the one you meant to get. Completing three weeks late must not produce an occurrence one week away.

Same lateness, same rule shape, opposite answer. Schedule-anchored ignores the completion date entirely. This case exists to be run alongside the one above: a tool that returns the same value for both has not implemented anchoring at all.
The whole span advances. A task available a day before it is due stays available a day before it is due.
The new due date derives from the completion; the available date derives from the gap, not from its own advance. Advancing both independently from the completion date collapses the span.

The series ends by counting instances, not by reading a counter carried on the rule. An occurrence index stored inside the rule object is instance state hiding in a rule, and every code path that copies or edits a rule then has to remember to preserve it. One that forgets restarts the series silently.
The end date is inclusive. An occurrence falling exactly on it is generated.

Bi-weekly intervals anchor to the series start, not to whichever date is being advanced from. Implementations that count week offsets from the current instance re-phase the series whenever an instance is rescheduled.

A weekday pattern describes positions in a calendar; completion anchoring describes an interval since an event. Combining them has no coherent answer — completing on a Thursday would yield next Wednesday, six days later, which is neither the pattern nor the interval. Producers wanting interval-from-completion should use freq=daily with an interval in days.

A monthly rule that does not say which day it recurs on can only be interpreted by looking at an instance — and the instance may already have been clamped to the 28th, in which case the rule reads as a rule about the 28th and the original intent is gone. A rule has to be readable on its own. This is what makes `monthEnd: clamp` implementable at all: clamping without knowing the day you are clamping *from* is just moving to the end of the month.
